Map runs `iterator` for each item from `items_path`, with optional `max_concurrency`, and the result is a list. Succeed finishes with the current data. Fail finishes with `error` and `cause`.

A task, wait, pass, parallel, or map without `next` is treated as `end: true`. The schema sets `end` in that case. Every state can have a `comment`.

JSON paths are `$`, `$.a.b`, `$.items[0]`, and `$['key']`. `input_path` selects what the task receives. The default is `$`. `result_path` of `$` replaces the state data with the result. `$.payment` stores the result under that key. `null` discards the result. The schema default for `result_path` is `$`.

Retry `errors` are exception class names. `"*"` or `States.ALL` means any. Defaults in the schema and the doc are `max_attempts` 3, `interval_seconds` 1, and `backoff_rate` 2.0. `max_delay_seconds` is optional. The first matching retrier is used. When retries are exhausted, the first matching catcher routes to `next`. A catch `result_path` defaults to `$.error` and stores `error` and `cause`. With no match the run fails. A rule whose variable is missing or the wrong type is false, not a failure.

Sources: `docs/workflows.md#state-types`, `docs/workflows.md#data-flow`, `docs/workflows.md#retry-and-catch`, `src/py_serverless_kit/config/schema.py`

```text
choices:
  - {variable: "$.status", equals: "paid", next: Ship}
  - {variable: "$.amount", gte: 100, next: Review}
  - and:
      - {variable: "$.country", in: [IN, US]}
      - not: {variable: "$.vip", equals: true}
    next: Standard
  - or: [{variable: "$.email", is_present: false}, {variable: "$.email", is_null: true}]
    next: AskEmail
```

title: Concept: workflows
text:
# Concept: workflows

A workflow chains functions with branching, retries, waits, parallel branches, and fan-out. You define it once under `workflows` in pskit.yml. pskit runs it natively as AWS Step Functions, Google Cloud Workflows, or, when you set `engine: native`, Azure Logic Apps. Every other target uses the embedded engine inside an auto-generated `<workflow>-orchestrator` function. On premises that function runs inside the long-lived host, so the workflow is not cut off by a function timeout. `pskit workflow run` uses the same embedded engine locally.

Required keys are `start_at` (it must name a state) and `states`. `description` defaults to an empty string. `engine` defaults to `auto`: native on aws and gcp, embedded elsewhere, including Azure until you opt in. `native` is an error on a cloud without a native engine. `embedded` forces the embedded engine everywhere. `enabled` defaults to true. False keeps the workflow in the file and skips it on deploy. `timeout` is the AWS TimeoutSeconds, the embedded orchestrator function timeout capped at the provider maximum, and a limit the embedded engine enforces by ending the run `TIMED_OUT`.

`options.type` is AWS only: `STANDARD` or `EXPRESS`, default `STANDARD`. `options.http` is embedded only and defaults to true. False removes the orchestrator's HTTP trigger. `options.start_on_entry` is on premises only and defaults to true. `options.sync` is Azure native only and defaults to true. False drops the Response actions so the caller gets 202 at once.

Every `next`, `default`, and `catch.next` must name a state. Every `function` must exist under `functions`. Task handlers receive `event.type == "workflow"` and the state input in `event.data`. Their return value is the task result. Error names in `retry` and `catch` are the Python exception class names the handler raises.

Sources: `docs/workflows.md#workflows-state-machines`, `docs/workflows.md#workflow-keys`, `src/py_serverless_kit/config/schema.py`

```text
functions:
  validate: {handler: app.orders.validate}
  charge:   {handler: app.orders.charge}
  notify:   {handler: app.orders.notify}

workflows:
  order-pipeline:
    description: Validate, charge and notify
    start_at: Validate
    states:
      Validate:
        type: task
        function: validate
        retry: [{errors: [TimeoutError], max_attempts: 3, interval_seconds: 2, backoff_rate: 2}]
        catch: [{errors: [ValueError], next: Rejected}]
        next: Route
      Route:
        type: choice
        choices:
          - {variable: "$.amount", gt: 1000, next: ManualReview}
        default: Charge
      ManualReview: {type: wait, seconds: 3600, next: Charge}
      Charge:       {type: task, function: charge, result_path: "$.payment", next: Notify}
      Notify:       {type: task, function: notify, result_path: null, end: true}
      Rejected:     {type: fail, error: OrderRejected, cause: validation failed}
```

text:
# Example: 01-hello-http

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.yml, requirements.txt.

Comments in pskit.yml: Minimal service: one function, one HTTP route. Per-cloud overrides. A block is applied only when that provider is selected (e.g. `pskit deploy --provider gcp`); the handler code never changes.

## The YAML

`providers:` holds per-cloud overrides (region, project id, ...). They only apply when
that cloud is selected, so one file serves every target.

## Deploy

`pskit deploy` prints the URL, e.g. `GET https://abc123.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/hello`.

title: Example: 02-rest-api
text:
# Example: 02-rest-api

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.yml, requirements.txt.

Comments in pskit.yml: Allowed browser origins for CORS - defined once, reused below. Gateway-level JWT validation is an AWS feature. On other clouds the route is public and the handler checks the Authorization header itself. Overrides replace lists instead of merging them, so the whole `events` list is restated.

# 02 · REST API

A CRUD API for books that uses every HTTP feature of the portable runtime.

| Feature | How |
| --- | --- |
| Path params `{id}` | `event.http.path_params["id"]` |
| Query string | `event.http.query.get("author")` |
| JSON body, automatic 400 on malformed JSON | `event.http.json()` |
| Validation errors with details | `raise BadRequest("...", details={...})` |
| 404 / 409 | `raise NotFound(...)`, `raise Conflict(...)` |
| Status code + headers | `Response.json(obj, status=201, headers={...})` |
| 204 | `Response.no_content()` |
| Binary responses | `Response.binary(png_bytes, "image/png")` |
| Redirects | `Response.redirect(url)` |
| Cookies | `resp.set_cookie(...)`, `event.http.cookies` |
| CORS (incl. preflight) | `cors:` on the http event |
| JWT auth | `auth: jwt` + `authorizer:` (AWS API Gateway) |

Unhandled exceptions become `500 {"error": "Internal Server Error", "request_id": ...}`.
The real message stays in the logs unless you set `PSKIT_DEBUG=1`.

> **Storage:** `app/store.py` keeps data in memory so the example is self-contained.
> Serverless instances don't share memory and are recycled at any time, so use a real
> database (DynamoDB, Firestore, Cosmos DB, PostgreSQL, ...) in production.

## The YAML

- `custom.cors` is defined once and reused with `${self:custom.cors}`.
- `admin-stats` uses `auth: jwt`. **Portability note:** gateway-level JWT validation is
  AWS-only. The `providers.gcp` / `providers.azure` blocks swap that route for a public one,
  and the handler then requires the `Authorization` header. Running `pskit validate --provider <cloud>`
  reports any setting a cloud does not support, before you deploy.

## Run locally

Or without a server:

## Deploy

On GCP every function gets its own URL, because there is no shared gateway. The runtime
still matches `/books/{id}` against the request path, so `event.http.path_params` works
the same way.

title: Example: 03-scheduled-jobs
text:
# Example: 03-scheduled-jobs

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.yml, requirements.txt.

Comments in pskit.yml: 

# 03 · Scheduled jobs

Shows cron and rate schedules with input payloads, time zones, schedules you can disable,
and a long job that stops gracefully before its timeout.

## Schedule syntax

| YAML | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `- schedule: 5 minutes` | every 5 minutes (`minute(s)`, `hour(s)`, `day(s)`) |
| `- schedule: "0 9 * * 1-5"` | standard 5-field cron |
| `input: {...}` | delivered to the handler as `event.data` |
| `timezone: Europe/Berlin` | IANA zone for cron evaluation |
| `enabled: false` | keep the trigger but pause it |

You always write **standard** cron. pskit translates it per cloud:

| Cloud | `cron: "0 9 * * 1-5"` becomes |
| --- | --- |
| AWS EventBridge Scheduler | `cron(0 9 ? * 2-6 *)` (day-of-week 1-7, `?` rules) |
| GCP Cloud Scheduler | `0 9 * * 1-5` |
| Azure timer trigger | `0 0 9 * * 1-5` (seconds first) |
| Alibaba / Huawei | `0 0 9 * * 1-5` |
| Tencent | `0 0 9 * * 1-5 *` |

**Time zones** are honoured on AWS and GCP. Azure Linux consumption plans run timers in UTC,
so set the cron in UTC there (use a `providers.azure` override if needed).

**Rates** must convert to cron on clouds that only accept cron, so use a divisor of 60
minutes or 24 hours (`5 minutes`, `6 hours`, ...). `pskit validate` flags rates that don't
convert.

## Run locally

Expected (abridged):

## Deploy

Turn the cleanup off in one stage without touching code: `CLEANUP_ENABLED=false pskit deploy`.

title: Example: 04-queue-worker
text:
# Example: 04-queue-worker

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.yml, requirements.txt.

Comments in pskit.yml: fifo: true              # ordered, exactly-once processing (AWS SQS FIFO only)

# 04 · Queue worker

Shows a batch consumer that retries only the failed messages, a dead-letter queue with its
own consumer, and an HTTP producer.

## How a batch is handled

| Cloud | What `BatchResult` does |
| --- | --- |
| AWS SQS | partial batch response: only failed messages are retried |
| On-premises | partial batch response: only failed messages are retried, then dead-lettered |
| GCP Pub/Sub, Azure Storage Queues, others | any failure fails the invocation, so the whole batch is redelivered |

Make processing **idempotent**: on most clouds a message can be delivered more than once.

## Queue options

| Option | AWS | GCP | Azure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | SQS queue | Pub/Sub topic + push subscription | Storage queue |
| `batch_size` | yes | ignored (one message per invocation) | host setting |
| `dead_letter` / `max_receive` | SQS redrive policy | warning, not configured | poison queue `<name>-poison` (built in) |
| `fifo` | SQS FIFO | warning | not supported |
| `existing: true` | look up instead of create | yes | yes |

On premises every option in the YAML is implemented by a directory of message files. `builtin` (the default) creates that directory at start. `{use: directory, path: ...}` under `provider.options.services.queue` uses a directory you already have.

`pskit validate --provider <cloud>` prints the warnings for your configuration.

## The producer

Publishing a message is a cloud SDK call: `boto3` `sqs.send_message`, `google-cloud-pubsub`
`publish`, `azure-storage-queue` `send_message`. py-serverless-kit does **not** wrap these
SDKs, because their delivery guarantees and options differ too much. Keep that one call
behind your own small interface, for example:

The example's `enqueue` handler logs on a cloud, so it runs anywhere without credentials. On premises (`PSKIT_ONPREM_ROOT`) it writes the job into the file queue with `submit_queue`.

## Run locally

Expected: the transient failure is reported and the poison message is dropped.

title: Example: 05-storage-events
text:
# Example: 05-storage-events

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.yml, requirements.txt.

Comments in pskit.yml: Bucket names are global on AWS/GCP: make them unique per account and stage. Azure blob triggers fire on created/updated blobs only. Deletions need an Event Grid subscription, so on Azure the function is deployed without a trigger (invoke-only) - wire Event Grid separately if you need it. A blob trigger on a container outside the Function App's storage account needs a connection string - here we listen to an app-owned container instead. The shared audit bucket is not on this machine. Create a local directory bucket with the host so the function has somewhere to listen.

# 05 · Storage events

Shows functions triggered by objects being created or deleted, prefix/suffix filters, and
listening to a bucket that some other system owns.

## Record fields (same on every cloud)

| Field | Example |
| --- | --- |
| `record.bucket` | `storage-events-data-demo-1234-dev` |
| `record.key` | `incoming/sales 2026.csv` (already URL-decoded) |
| `record.size` | `1048576` |
| `record.action` | `created` or `deleted` |
| `record.raw` | the provider's native record, if you need more |

## The YAML

- `existing: true` looks the bucket up instead of creating it. `pskit remove` never deletes it.
- Bucket names are global on AWS and GCP. `custom.bucket` therefore adds the stage
  (`${opt:stage}`), and you can set your own prefix with `DATA_BUCKET`.

| Cloud | created | deleted | prefix/suffix filter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AWS S3 | yes | yes | native |
| GCP Cloud Storage | yes | yes | applied by the runtime (Eventarc can't filter keys) |
| Azure Blob | yes | **no** (needs Event Grid) | blob path pattern |

On GCP a function with several storage triggers is deployed as one Cloud Function per
trigger. You still see a single logical function in `pskit info` and the dashboard.

# 06 · Pub/Sub topic fan-out One topic with two subscribers: every message goes to both.

One subscriber uses a filter
policy so it only receives `order.shipped` events.

## The YAML

| Cloud | Topic | Subscription | `filter` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AWS | SNS topic | Lambda subscription per function | SNS filter policy (native) |
| GCP | Pub/Sub topic | Eventarc trigger per function | not configured, so the handler filters |
| Azure | Service Bus topic | one subscription per function | warning, so the handler filters |

Because filters are not available everywhere, `notify_customer` repeats the check in code
(`_wants`). Doing that in your own handlers keeps them correct on every cloud.

Use `existing: true` to subscribe to a topic owned by another service. On Azure that also
needs `options.servicebus_namespace_id` and `options.servicebus_connection`.

title: Example: 07-workflow-orders
text:
# Example: 07-workflow-orders

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.yml, requirements.txt. Comments in pskit.yml:
# 07 · Order workflow (Step Functions, portable) An order pipeline that uses

**every state type**, written once and compiled to: | Cloud | Engine | Deployed as | | --- | --- | --- | | AWS | native | AWS Step Functions state machine (ASL) | | GCP | native | Google Cloud Workflows | | Azure and the other 7 clouds | embedded | an extra `order-pipeline-orchestrator` function running the pskit engine |
## State types used | Type | State | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | `task` |

Validate, Charge, ReserveItem, Confirm, Ship | `function:` is a function name from `functions:` | | `choice` | Route | `and` / `or` / `not`, numeric `gt`, string `equals` | | `wait` | ManualReview | `seconds` or `seconds_path` | | `pass` | Invoice | injects `result` at `result_path` | | `map` | Reserve | `items_path`, `iterator`, `max_concurrency` | | `parallel` | Fulfil | list of `branches`, the result is a list | | `succeed` / `fail` | Done / Declined / Rejected | `error` + `cause` | **Data flow:** every state receives the whole document (`input_path` narrows it). A task's return value is stored at `result_path`: `$` replaces the document, `$.payment` adds a field, and `null` discards the result. **Errors:** an exception's **class name** is its error name. `retry: [{errors: [PaymentGatewayTimeout]}]` and `catch: [{errors: [PaymentDeclined]}]` work the same way on Step Functions, Cloud Workflows and the embedded engine. Use `*` to match everything. Choice operators: `equals`, `not_equals`, `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `in`, `contains`, `matches` (glob), `is_null`, `is_present`, plus `and` / `or` / `not`. > AWS Step Functions fails a choice that reads a missing field. That's why `validate-order` > normalises the order (fills in `customer.vip`, `currency`, `channel`) before `Route` reads it.
## Run locally (embedded engine) Wait states are skipped locally unless you pass

`--sleep`. Expected output of the happy path (abridged):
## Deploy Start an execution: - **AWS:** `aws stepfunctions start-execution

--state-machine-arn <arn from pskit info> --input file://events/happy.json` - **GCP:** `gcloud workflows run order-workflow-dev-order-pipeline --data="$(cat events/happy.json)"` - **Embedded engine:** `POST <endpoint>/workflows/order-pipeline` with the JSON input. The response is `{"status": "SUCCEEDED", "output": ...}`, or HTTP 500 with `error` / `cause`.
### Native vs embedded

The embedded engine runs the whole workflow **inside one function invocation**. Its tasks are called in-process, because they live in the same bundle.

title: Example: 08-multi-cloud
text:
# Example: 08-multi-cloud

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.aws.yml, pskit.azure.yml, pskit.gcp.yml, pskit.yml, requirements.txt. Comments in pskit.yml: One file for every provider, including an on-premises host. Pick the target with: pskit deploy -> provider.name below (aws) pskit deploy --provider gcp -> applies providers.gcp on top Everything under `providers.<cloud>` is merged over the base config only when that cloud is selected. Top-level ProviderConfig keys (region, runtime, timeout, options, ...) may be written directly under the cloud name.
# 08 · Multi-cloud: same code, every provider `app/handlers.py` deploys unchanged to all

eleven providers, including an on-premises host. Only the configuration differs, and you can organise it in either of two ways.
## Option A: one file with `providers:` overrides `pskit.yml` holds the shared definition

plus a `providers.<cloud>` block per cloud:
## Option B: one small file per cloud with `extends:`

Each child file names the cloud in `provider.name` and sets its own values under `providers.<cloud>`, so they take precedence over the parent's block for that cloud. Every combination gets its own Terraform workspace (`.pskit/<provider>-<stage>/`), so the same service can be live on several clouds at once. `pskit dashboard` then shows all of them on one page.
## What each cloud needs | Cloud | Tier | Required settings | Notes | | --- |

| --- | --- | | aws | stable | AWS credentials | HTTP API, EventBridge Scheduler | | gcp | stable | `options.project` | Cloud Functions gen2, Cloud Scheduler | | azure | stable | `options.subscription_id` | Function App (Linux consumption) | | alibaba | beta | `ALICLOUD_*` credentials | FC 3.0 HTTP + timer triggers | | tencent | beta | `TENCENTCLOUD_*` credentials | SCF + API Gateway; Python 3.9/3.10 | | huawei | beta | `options.apig_instance_id` | FunctionGraph + dedicated APIG | | oracle | experimental | `compartment_id`, `subnet_ids`, `image` or `image_repository` | container images; no schedules | | ibm | beta | `IC_API_KEY` | Code Engine functions; HTTP only, Python 3.11, max 120 s | | digitalocean | beta | `options.namespace`, `doctl` on PATH | deployed with `doctl serverless` | | cloudflare | experimental | `options.account_id` | Python Workers (stdlib + Pyodide packages only) | | onprem | experimental | nothing (optional `options.port`) | a Python process on this machine; queues, storage and topics are directories | Where a cloud lacks a feature, the override says so explicitly. For example `functions.ticker.events: []` on IBM and Oracle deploys `ticker` without a schedule instead of failing.

title: Example: 09-function-invoke
text:
# Example: 09-function-invoke

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.yml, requirements.txt.

Comments in pskit.yml: On AWS invoke() needs lambda:InvokeFunction on the sibling functions. Their names are <service>-<stage>-<function>. invoke() calls https://<region>-<project>.cloudfunctions.net/<name> with an ID token. The functions share pskit's invoker service account. Azure has no SDK-level "invoke function" API, so give the caller the URLs. Fill them in from `pskit info` after the first deploy (or in CI).

# 09 · Function-to-function invoke

`quote` (HTTP) calls two internal functions by their logical names:

The target sees `event.type == "invoke"` and `event.data == payload`.

## How each cloud resolves the target

`invoke()` tries these in order:

1. **`PSKIT_ENDPOINT_<NAME>`** env var set (name upper-cased, `-` becomes `_`): HTTP POST to that
   URL. This works on **every** cloud and always wins.
2. **local** (`pskit invoke`, `pskit dev`, tests): in-process call, no network.
3. **AWS:** `lambda:Invoke` via boto3 on `<service>-<stage>-<name>`. boto3 is preinstalled in
   the Lambda runtime. The role needs `lambda:InvokeFunction`, granted in `provider.iam` here.
   `asynchronous=True` uses `InvocationType=Event`.
4. **GCP:** authenticated HTTPS call to `https://<region>-<project>.cloudfunctions.net/<name>`
   with an ID token from the metadata server.
5. **Everything else:** raises `InvokeError` and tells you which `PSKIT_ENDPOINT_*` variable to set.

| Cloud | Setup needed |
| --- | --- |
| AWS | IAM statement (shown in `pskit.yml`) |
| GCP | none |
| Azure, Alibaba, Tencent, Huawei, Oracle, IBM, DigitalOcean, Cloudflare | set `PSKIT_ENDPOINT_<NAME>` in the caller's `environment` (URL from `pskit info`) |

On Azure an invoke-only function is exposed at `/_pskit/invoke/<name>` and protected by a
function key. Put that URL, including `?code=<key>`, into `PRICE_CALCULATOR_URL` /
`AUDIT_LOG_URL` and redeploy. The `providers.azure` block wires them up.

> Prefer queues/topics (examples 04 and 06) for work that may be retried or slow.
> Use `invoke()` for quick request/response calls, and workflows (example 07) for multi-step processes.

## Run locally

title: Example: 10-stages-and-config
text:
# Example: 10-stages-and-config

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.yml, requirements.txt.

Comments in pskit.yml: Reusable values. Read anywhere with ${self:custom.<key>}. Secrets: never commit them. Inject from CI / a secret manager at deploy time: Per-stage overrides: deep-merged over everything above when --stage matches.

# 10 · Stages, variables and secrets

Shows one config with dev / staging / prod stages, every variable source, local `.env`
files, and how to handle secrets.

## Variables

| Syntax | Resolves to |
| --- | --- |
| `${env:NAME}` | environment variable; error if unset |
| `${env:NAME, default}` | environment variable or the default |
| `${opt:stage}` / `${opt:region}` / `${opt:provider}` | effective CLI values |
| `${self:path.to.value}` | any value in the merged config, e.g. `${self:custom.table}` |
| `${file(config/limits.json)}` | parsed JSON / YAML, or raw text for other files |
| `${tf:aws_x.y.attr}` | left for Terraform (example 11) |
| anything else, e.g. `${aws:username}` | kept verbatim (IAM policy variables) |

A value that is *only* a variable keeps its type, so
`memory: "${self:custom.limits.prod.memory}"` is the number `1024`.

## Precedence (later wins)

1. `extends:` parent files
2. this file
3. `providers.<cloud>`
4. `stages.<stage>`
5. CLI flags `--provider`, `--stage`, `--region`

Overrides deep-merge mappings and replace lists.

## Run locally

Expected output (dev, with `.env`):

`.env` overrides the YAML locally. `TABLE_NAME` is therefore `local-orders` instead of
`shop-config-dev-orders`.

## Deploy each stage

Each stage is fully isolated: its own resource names (`shop-config-prod-config`) and its
own Terraform state (`.pskit/aws-prod/`, or the S3 backend configured for prod).

## Secrets

- **Never commit secrets** to `pskit.yml` or `.env`. Both `.env` and `.env.*` are excluded from
  bundles, and `pskit init` git-ignores `.env`.
- `${env:SECRET}` at deploy time (from CI secrets) is the simplest option. The value ends
  up as a function environment variable, which is visible to anyone with read access to the function.
- Better: store the secret in the cloud's secret manager and pass only its **reference**:

  Then read the value at cold start with the cloud SDK. GCP Secret Manager and Azure Key
  Vault references follow the same pattern.

title: Example: 11-custom-terraform
text:
# Example: 11-custom-terraform

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.yml, requirements.txt.

Comments in pskit.yml: ${tf:...} is passed to Terraform untouched -> the real table name after apply. Remote state: required for teams and CI so everyone shares one state file. Create the bucket (versioning on) and lock table once, outside this service. Raw Terraform JSON, deep-merged into the generated main.tf.json. On this machine there is no DynamoDB table and no S3 state bucket. The handler already uses an in-memory repository when PSKIT_PROVIDER is not aws. Shell commands run from the project root. PSKIT_SERVICE, PSKIT_STAGE, PSKIT_PROVIDER and PSKIT_WORK_DIR are set for them.

# 11 · Custom Terraform, remote state and hooks

pskit generates Terraform for functions and triggers. Everything else your service needs
(databases, secrets, buckets with special policies, ...) you add as **raw Terraform** in the
same file, and wire it up with `${tf:...}` references.

## `terraform.extra`

`extra` is Terraform JSON syntax,
deep-merged into the generated `.pskit/<provider>-<stage>/main.tf.json`. It can add
`resource`, `data`, `output`, `locals` and `module` blocks, or override generated attributes.

## `${tf:...}` references

User-supplied strings are escaped so that `${...}` can't accidentally become a Terraform
expression. `${tf:<expression>}` is the explicit opt-in: In the generated Terraform these become `${aws_dynamodb_table.orders.name}`, and Terraform
orders the resources accordingly (table first, then the Lambda).

## Remote state

`provider.state` configures a Terraform backend.
Use one for any shared environment, so CI and teammates see the same state:

| Cloud | backend | config keys |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AWS | `s3` | `bucket`, `key`, `region`, `dynamodb_table` (locking), `encrypt` |
| GCP | `gcs` | `bucket`, `prefix` |
| Azure | `azurerm` | `resource_group_name`, `storage_account_name`, `container_name`, `key` |
| any | `http`, `remote` (Terraform Cloud), `pg`, ... | see the Terraform docs |

Without `state`, the state lives in `.pskit/<provider>-<stage>/terraform.tfstate` on your
machine, which is fine for experiments only.

## Hooks

`hooks.before_package`, `after_package`, `before_deploy`, `after_deploy`, `before_remove`
and `after_remove` run shell commands from the project root. A failing command aborts
the deploy. Here, the tests must pass before deploying, and a smoke test runs against the
new endpoint afterwards (`scripts/smoke_test.py` reads `$PSKIT_WORK_DIR/deployment.json`).

## Run locally

Locally the repository falls back to memory, so no AWS credentials are needed.

## Deploy

This example is AWS-specific by nature, because `extra` contains AWS resources. For
another cloud, add that cloud's resources (e.g. `google_firestore_database`,
`azurerm_cosmosdb_account`) under `providers.<cloud>.terraform.extra` and add one
repository class in `app/repository.py`. The handlers stay the same.

title: Example: 12-async-and-context
text:
# Example: 12-async-and-context

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.yml, requirements.txt.

Comments in pskit.yml: 

## Async

Any handler can be `async def`. The runtime awaits it, so you can use `asyncio.gather`,
`httpx.AsyncClient`, `asyncpg` and similar libraries directly. The handler signature is
`handler(event, ctx)` or just `handler(event)`.

## Context

| Attribute | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ctx.request_id` | platform request id (Lambda request id, Azure invocation id, ...) |
| `ctx.function` / `ctx.service` / `ctx.stage` / `ctx.region` / `ctx.provider` | where you are |
| `ctx.memory_mb` | configured memory, when the platform reports it |
| `ctx.remaining_time_ms()` | ms until the platform kills the invocation; `None` if unknown |
| `ctx.logger` | structured logger bound to function / request id / provider |
| `ctx.env` | `os.environ` |
| `ctx.raw` | the native context object, as an escape hatch |

`event.to_dict()` gives a compact, JSON-safe summary of any event, which is ideal for logs.

## Logging

In the cloud this produces one JSON line:

Locally the CLI switches to readable text (`PSKIT_LOG_FORMAT=text`). Control the level with
`LOG_LEVEL`.

## Run locally

Expected (abridged):

Locally `remaining_time_ms()` is `null`. On AWS, Azure and the others it counts down
from the configured timeout.

title: Example: 13-migrate-from-aws-lambda
text:
# Example: 13-migrate-from-aws-lambda

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md. Comments in pskit.yml: AFTER: replaces before/template.yaml AND before/state_machine.asl.json. step 2: switch clouds by adding a block and running `pskit deploy --provider gcp`
# 13 · Migrating AWS Lambda + Step Functions to any cloud `before/` is a typical

AWS-only service: Lambda handlers that parse API Gateway / SQS events by hand, a SAM template and a hand-written ASL state machine. `after/` is the same service on py-serverless-kit. It deploys to AWS first, unchanged in behaviour, and then to GCP, Azure or any other supported cloud by changing the provider.
## Step 1 · Inventory what you have For every Lambda, list its trigger (API Gateway route,

SQS, S3, SNS, schedule, Step Functions task, direct invoke) and the AWS APIs it calls. Each trigger maps 1:1 to a pskit event: | AWS | pskit.yml | | --- | --- | | API Gateway `POST /orders` | `- http: POST /orders` | | SQS event source mapping | `- queue: {name: ..., batch_size: 10}` | | S3 notification | `- storage: {bucket: ..., events: [created], prefix: ...}` | | SNS subscription | `- topic: name` | | EventBridge schedule | `- schedule: "0 9 * * *"` or `- schedule: 5 minutes` | | Step Functions task | a function without events + a `workflows:` task state | | `lambda.invoke(...)` | `invoke("function-name", payload)` |
## Step 2 · Strip the event plumbing out of the handlers | Before | After | |

| --- | | `json.loads(base64...(event["body"]))` | `event.http.json()` | | `event["pathParameters"]["id"]` | `event.http.path_params["id"]` | | `event["queryStringParameters"]` | `event.http.query` | | `return {"statusCode": 400, "body": json.dumps(...)}` | `raise BadRequest(...)` | | `return {"statusCode": 202, "body": ...}` | `return data, 202` or `Response.json(data, 202)` | | `for r in event["Records"]: json.loads(r["body"])` | `for r in event.records: r.json()` | | `{"batchItemFailures": [...]}` | `BatchResult().fail(record)` | | task Lambda `event` (raw state) | `event.data` | | `context.aws_request_id` | `ctx.request_id` | | `print(...)` | `ctx.logger.info(..., extra={...})` | Business logic stays where it was. Diff `before/lambda_function.py` against `after/app/orders.py` to see how little changes.

title: Example: 14-testing
text:
# Example: 14-testing

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, ci.github-workflow.yml, pskit.yml, requirements.txt.

Comments in pskit.yml: 

# 14 · Testing handlers and workflows

Handlers are plain Python functions, and the kit ships helpers that run them through the
**same dispatcher** the clouds use. Tests therefore cover routing, error mapping (400/404/500),
CORS and batch results without deploying anything.

| Tool | Use for |
| --- | --- |
| `LocalRunner(project).invoke(name, event)` | full dispatcher: env vars from `pskit.yml`, routing, error → status mapping |
| `http_event(method, path, body, headers, query)` | synthetic HTTP request (query string in `path` works) |
| `build_event("queue" / "topic" / "storage" / "schedule" / "invoke", data)` | synthetic event; a list of items becomes several records |
| `Event(...)` / `Record(...)` | full control, e.g. message attributes |
| `runner.run_workflow(name, input)` | whole workflow with the real task handlers (`output` + `history`) |
| `WorkflowEngine(definition, task_runner)` | state-machine logic with stubbed tasks |

HTTP functions return a `Response` (`resp.status`, `resp.render()` → `(status, headers, bytes)`).
Other functions return whatever the handler returned.

## CI

`ci.github-workflow.yml` is a ready-made GitHub Actions workflow with two jobs: 1. **test:** unit tests on several Python versions;
2. **validate:** `pskit validate` + `pskit package` for AWS, GCP and Azure on every pull
   request. A change that would break deployment to any target cloud fails the build,
   and the generated Terraform is uploaded for review.

Copy it to `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. Deployment itself is covered in example 15.

title: Example: 15-ci-cd-deploy
text:
# Example: 15-ci-cd-deploy

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, deploy.github-workflow.yml, pskit.yml, requirements.txt.

Comments in pskit.yml: One state file per stage, shared by CI and humans.

# 15 · CI/CD: deploy per stage from GitHub Actions

`deploy.github-workflow.yml` is a complete pipeline:

| Trigger | Deploys |
| --- | --- |
| push to `main` | `dev` |
| tag `v*` | `staging`, then `prod` (after a manual approval on the `prod` environment) |
| manual run | any stage you pick |

Each deploy job does the following:

1. authenticates with **OIDC**, so there are no long-lived cloud keys in GitHub;
2. `pskit validate --stage <stage>`;
3. `pskit deploy --stage <stage>`: Terraform plan + apply against **remote state**;
4. smoke-tests `GET /health` using the endpoint from `pskit info --json`;
5. uploads the dashboard (`.pskit/dashboard/index.html`) and the deployment record as build artifacts.

## One-time setup (AWS)

1. **State bucket + lock table** (once per account):
2. **OIDC role:** add the GitHub OIDC provider (`token.actions.githubusercontent.com`) to IAM
   and create a role whose trust policy allows `repo:<org>/<repo>:environment:<stage>`.
   Grant it the permissions Terraform needs (Lambda, API Gateway, IAM roles for the
   service, CloudWatch Logs, plus SQS/SNS/S3/Step Functions if you use them).
3. **GitHub:** create environments `dev`, `staging`, `prod` (add reviewers to `prod`), and set
   the variables `AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN`, `TF_STATE_BUCKET` and `TF_LOCK_TABLE`.

## GCP / Azure

The workflow contains commented steps for both:

- **GCP:** `google-github-actions/auth@v2` with Workload Identity Federation; state in a GCS
  bucket (`providers.gcp.state` in `pskit.yml`). Deploy with `pskit deploy --provider gcp`.
- **Azure:** `azure/login@v2` with a federated credential; Terraform needs
  `ARM_USE_OIDC=true`, `ARM_CLIENT_ID`, `ARM_TENANT_ID` and `ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID`. State goes in a
  storage account (`providers.azure.state`).

## Why remote state matters

Terraform state records which cloud resources belong to this service. With the default
local state (`.pskit/<provider>-<stage>/terraform.tfstate`), every CI run would start empty
and try to create everything again. The `state:` block points every run, and every
developer, at the same file, and the lock table prevents two applies at once.

## Try it locally

title: Example: 16-on-premises
text:
# Example: 16-on-premises

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.yml, requirements.txt.

Comments in pskit.yml: On-premises deploy: one Python process on this machine. Missing queues, buckets and topics are created as directories at start. Point a service at a directory you already have with `use: directory`. Blob triggers fire on created blobs only.

# 16 · On-premises

Same handlers as a cloud deploy, running as one Python process on this machine.
`pskit deploy` starts that process. HTTP is served directly. Schedules, queues,
storage and topics run inside the process when you do not already have those
services.

## What gets created

| Service | This example | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| schedule | `builtin` | in the host process |
| queue | `builtin` | `.pskit/onprem-data/on-prem-demo-dev/queues` |
| topic | `builtin` | `.pskit/onprem-data/on-prem-demo-dev/topics` |
| storage | `directory` | `.onprem/buckets` (a folder you can point at an existing tree) |
| workflow | `embedded` | the host calls the task functions in-process |

`pskit remove` stops the process and leaves those directories in place.

To use a directory you already have: `existing: true` on one queue, bucket or topic means "do not create it; wait until
that directory appears".

## Run

Publish into the services the host is running:

From a handler in the same process, `submit_queue`, `submit_topic`, `put_object`
and `delete_object` in `py_serverless_kit.runtime.onprem_host` write to the same
directories. They are available when `PSKIT_ONPREM_ROOT` is set. Example 04 uses
that for its HTTP producer.

Set `options.admin_token` and send `x-pskit-token` on `/__pskit/*` except
`/__pskit/health`. Each example uses its own port so several hosts can run at once.

`pskit dev` is still the hot-reloading HTTP server. This example is the durable
deploy: it keeps running after `pskit deploy` returns.

To copy the same host onto another machine (SSH, Docker, or a bundled CPython
when that machine has no Python), see 17-on-premises-remote.

title: Example: 17-on-premises-remote
text:
# Example: 17-on-premises-remote

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.yml, requirements.txt. Comments in pskit.yml: Remote on-premises deploy. This file ships the function bundle to a Linux server that may not have Python. `python: bundle` downloads a portable CPython at apply time and copies it with the app. `install: systemd` keeps the host up across reboots. Required on the laptop: OpenSSH (`ssh`, `scp`). Required on the server: SSH access. Python on the server is optional. set PSKIT_ONPREM_HOST=192.0.2.10 pskit deploy Switch to Docker (image built on this machine, run on the server) by replacing deploy.method with docker and setting pem to the server .pem. pskit deploy asks for a .pem on a terminal when identity_file is empty (Enter keeps the SSH agent for method ssh). method: scp is the same archive copy as ssh. Docker on a server installs the engine when `docker` is missing, then waits until /__pskit/health answers. See the README.
# 17 · On-premises, remote server

Example 16 runs the host on the laptop that runs `pskit deploy`. This example copies the same kind of host onto a machine you SSH into — a factory box, a VM, or a rack server. The handler code does not change. Three ways to get code from this laptop onto that server: | `options.deploy.method` | What the server needs | What the laptop needs | When to use it | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `local` | this machine (example 16) | Python + pskit | laptop / the server *is* the deploy machine | | `ssh` or `scp` | SSH. Python only if `python: system` | OpenSSH (`ssh`, `scp`) and a `.pem` or the SSH agent | most on-prem Linux boxes | | `docker` | SSH. Docker is installed at deploy when it is missing | Docker CLI, OpenSSH, and a `.pem` for the server | the server should run a container, with or without Docker already installed | When the server has **no Python**, pick one of: - `method: ssh` (or `method: scp`) and `python: bundle` — pskit downloads a portable CPython (python-build-standalone) at apply time, packs it into one `release.tar.gz`, copies that file, and restarts systemd (this file) - `method: docker` — the image is `FROM python:3.12-slim` and is built on this machine. The server does not need Python.

An address or login copied from the source was rewritten in this card. Addresses use 192.0.2.0/24, a documentation range. The login in those examples is deploy.

text:
# Example: 18-resources

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.yml, requirements.txt.

Comments in pskit.yml: Services the functions use. Managed ones are created by pskit; `external: true` ones already exist and pskit only hands their details to the handlers. On-premises the same resources can live in services you already run: resources: jobs: external: true options: {driver: redis, url: "redis://127.0.0.1:6379/0"} uploads: external: true options: driver: s3 endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:9000 access_key: ${env:MINIO_ACCESS_KEY} secret_key: ${env:MINIO_SECRET_KEY}

# 18 · Resources: buckets, queues, topics and external services

`resources:` declares the services your functions use, once, for every cloud.

| Resource | Kind | What pskit does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `uploads` | managed storage | creates the bucket (no trigger needed) and grants access |
| `jobs` | managed queue | creates the queue; `worker` consumes it with `queue: {resource: jobs}` |
| `notifications` | managed topic | creates the topic and grants publish |
| `orders-db` | external database | creates nothing; passes host/port/database to `api` and `worker` |

Each bound function gets environment variables such as `PSKIT_RESOURCE_UPLOADS_NAME`
(plus `_ARN` / `_URL` / `_ID` where the provider knows them). Handlers read them with: Try it: Secrets: keep them out of `connection`. Store the *name* of a secret variable there
(`password_env`) and set the secret itself through your platform's secret store.

title: Example: 19-custom-drivers
text:
# Example: 19-custom-drivers

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.yml, requirements.txt. Comments in pskit.yml: Custom on-premises drivers: your own class feeds a queue or storage trigger. `driver: custom` + `class: "<module>:<Class>"` loads a class from this app. Every other option is passed to its constructor (`<name>_env: VAR` reads VAR from the host's environment first, so secrets stay out of generated files). Template drivers wrapping client libraries (add the library to requirements.txt): events: type: queue external: true options: {driver: custom, class: app.rabbitmq_queue:RabbitQueue, url_env: RABBITMQ_URL, queue: events} orders: type: queue external: true options: {driver: custom, class: app.kafka_queue:KafkaQueue, bootstrap_servers: "kafka:9092", topic: orders, group_id: workers} On a cloud the same resources are plain external queues / buckets (the custom classes are on-premises only); these blocks just make `--provider` switch cleanly.
# 19 · Custom on-premises drivers

When the queue or storage you already run has no built-in driver, write a small class and point a resource at it. The on-prem host still does the rest: polling, batching, `BatchResult` retries, dead-lettering, logs, stats and the dashboard. | Resource | Class | Backed by | | --- | --- | --- | | `jobs` | `app.backends:SqliteQueue` | one SQLite file, table `jobs` | | `jobs-dlq` | `app.backends:SqliteQueue` | the same file, table `jobs_dlq` | | `inbox` | `app.backends:FolderStorage` | a folder (works for NFS / SMB shares) | `app/rabbitmq_queue.py` (pika) and `app/kafka_queue.py` (kafka-python) are templates for brokers that need a client library. Both deliver at least once.
## The contract A **queue** class implements: | Method | Called | Must | | --- |

--- | --- | | `submit(body, attributes) -> id` | `submit_queue()`, `POST /__pskit/queues/<name>`, dead-lettering | store one message | | `claim(batch, visibility, now) -> [msg]` | every poll | reserve up to `batch` messages for `visibility` seconds; each `msg` has `id`, `body`, `attributes`, `receives`, `enqueued_at` (+ private `_keys` you need later) | | `settle(claimed, failed_ids, max_receive, dead_letter, now)` | after the handler | delete successes; make failures visible again; when `receives + 1 >= max_receive` and `dead_letter` is given, `dead_letter.submit(...)` then delete | | `depth() -> int` | stats / dashboard | messages waiting, or `-1` if unknown | | `recover(now, visibility)` | every few seconds | release reservations a crash left behind (no-op if the broker does it) | A **storage** class implements `scan() -> {key: (etag, size)}`, `put(key, data)`, `get(key) -> bytes` and `delete(key) -> bool`. The host diffs consecutive scans to fire `created` / `deleted`, so `etag` must change whenever the content changes.

title: Example: 20-onprem-external-clouds
text:
# Example: 20-onprem-external-clouds

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, pskit.yml, requirements.txt. Comments in pskit.yml: One on-premises host watching queues and buckets that live in other clouds. Every secret is given as `<name>_env: VARIABLE`: the host reads it from its own environment when it starts, so no key is written to pskit_host.json or Terraform state. A variable that is missing stops the host with an error naming it. Delete the resources (and their functions) you don't use; each one needs its credentials on the host before `pskit deploy`. ------------------------------------------------------------------ queues ------------------------------------------------------------------ storage Same shape for the other S3-compatible stores (swap the driver and its required keys): {driver: oss, region: cn-hangzhou} Alibaba OSS {driver: cos, region: ap-guangzhou} Tencent COS (bucket name ends in -<APPID>) {driver: obs, region: cn-north-4} Huawei OBS {driver: oci, region: eu-frankfurt-1, namespace: mytenancy} Oracle Object Storage {driver: ibm_cos, region: us-south} IBM Cloud Object Storage (HMAC keys) {driver: spaces, region: nyc3} DigitalOcean Spaces Queues without a built-in driver (RabbitMQ, Kafka, IBM MQ, OCI Queue, TDMQ, DMS): `driver: custom` - see examples/19-custom-drivers.
# 20 · On premises, watching other clouds

A single on-prem host consumes queues and watches buckets that live in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Alibaba Cloud, Cloudflare and a self-hosted MinIO. The handlers are ordinary pskit handlers. Retries (`BatchResult`), dead-lettering, logs, stats and the dashboard work the same as with the built-in queues. | Resource | Driver | Service | | --- | --- | --- | | `aws-jobs` | `sqs` | Amazon SQS | | `azure-jobs` | `azure_queue` | Azure Storage Queue | | `gcp-jobs` | `pubsub` | Google Pub/Sub (pull subscription) | | `alibaba-jobs` | `mns` | Alibaba Cloud MNS | | `cf-jobs` | `cloudflare_queue` | Cloudflare Queues | | `aws-media` | `aws` | Amazon S3 | | `azure-media` | `azure_blob` | Azure Blob Storage | | `gcp-media` | `gcs` | Google Cloud Storage | | `r2-media` | `r2` | Cloudflare R2 | | `minio-media` | `minio` | MinIO / Ceph | `pskit.yml` also lists the presets for Alibaba OSS, Tencent COS, Huawei OBS, Oracle Object Storage, IBM COS and DigitalOcean Spaces. For brokers without a built-in driver (RabbitMQ, Kafka, IBM MQ, OCI Queue, TDMQ, DMS), see `19-custom-drivers`.
## Credentials Secrets are referenced as `<name>_env: VARIABLE`, so the host reads them

from its own environment at start. Nothing secret is written to `pskit_host.json` or to Terraform state.

title: Example: 21-nodejs-typescript
text:
# Example: 21-nodejs-typescript

This directory is one of the examples that tests/test_examples.py packages and runs locally because it contains pskit.yml. Files here include README.md, package.json, pskit.yml, tsconfig.json.

Comments in pskit.yml: 

# 21 · Node.js + TypeScript

The same pskit features as the Python examples, with handlers written in TypeScript:
HTTP routes, a queue worker with partial batch failures, a schedule and a workflow.

## Files

| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `pskit.yml` | `runtime: nodejs20` makes this a Node.js service; handlers point at `src/*.ts` |
| `src/http.ts` | HTTP handlers (`hello`, `createOrder`, `getOrder`) |
| `src/jobs.ts` | queue consumer returning a `BatchResult`, scheduled report |
| `src/workflow.ts` | workflow tasks; `ValidationError` is caught by the workflow |
| `src/orders.ts` | shared logic, no cloud SDK |
| `tsconfig.json` | maps `pskit` to `.pskit/types/pskit/index.d.ts`, which pskit writes |
| `package.json` | your npm dependencies (none here) |

## The YAML

pskit compiles the `.ts` files with `tsc` when it packages or runs the service. Types for
`import { Response } from "pskit"` come from `.pskit/types/pskit/index.d.ts` (written by
`pskit init` / `pskit package`), so editors resolve them without installing anything.

## Run locally

Needs Node.js 18+ on PATH (and `tsc`, or `npx` to fetch it).

title: On-premises: Back up an on-premises service
text:
## Backups

`Backup` streams a dump out of the container into `.pskit/backups/` on this machine, or a folder you choose
(**Backup → Save to folder → Browse…**, remembered; CLI `--dir` / `-o`), also from an SSH server:

| Service | File | Restore |
|---|---|---|
| Redis / Valkey | `.rdb` | stop the container, copy it to `/data/dump.rdb` in the volume, start it |
| PostgreSQL | `.sql` | `psql -U pskit -f file.sql postgres` |
| MySQL / MariaDB | `.sql` | `mysql -uroot -p < file.sql` |
| MongoDB | `.archive` | `mongorestore --archive=file.archive -u pskit -p ... --authenticationDatabase admin` |
| RabbitMQ | `.definitions.json` | `rabbitmqctl import_definitions file.json` (messages are not included) |
| Kafka, NATS, MinIO | `.tar.gz` of the data directory | stop the container, extract into the volume, start it |

Data directories are copied while the service runs. For Kafka and NATS, stop producers first for a consistent copy.

These steps run on the on-premises provider. Saved servers are named once and then reused by deploy, services, and clusters. Open the matching studio page from the left navigation. Scaling cluster, Load balancers, Network map, and Resources are the pages for this work.

```
pskit validate
pskit resources onprem catalog
```

pskit resources onprem catalog lists the services and runtimes the create command can start. Passwords generated for a service are stored in the env file and under .pskit/, and they are left out of pskit.yml.

title: On-premises: pskit browsers for buckets and secrets
text:
## pskit's own browsers (when the native UI is missing)

Some services ship without a usable web UI. OpenBao's release images say *"OpenBao UI is not available in this
binary"*, and MinIO's community console no longer has the admin pages. For these, **Browse** on the service's row
opens pskit's UI in the studio:

| Service | Browser | What you can do |
|---|---|---|
| MinIO, RustFS, LocalStack, LocalEmu, Amazon S3 compatible | **Buckets (S3)** | Create and delete buckets (with every object and old version); folders and breadcrumbs; filter by name; 25 to 1000 objects per page with next / previous; upload several files (up to 64 MB each); download; info (size, type, ETag, metadata); old versions (list, download); rename / move and copy; share links valid 1 hour, 1 day or 7 days (S3 presigned URLs); bucket versioning on / off; bucket policy (private, public read, or your JSON) |
| fake-gcs-server | **Buckets (Cloud Storage)** | The same, without versioning, policies and signed links |
| OpenBao | **Secrets** | Folders, open a secret (values hidden until *Show values*), copy a value, versions (pick an old one), add / edit (each save is a new version), delete |
| LocalStack, LocalEmu, AWS Secrets Manager compatible | **Secrets (Secrets Manager)** | List with paging, open, add / edit, delete |

The studio talks to the service from your machine. When its port is closed by a firewall, it goes over the server's
SSH login instead (`127.0.0.1:<port>` on the server). Credentials stay in `.pskit/onprem-services.json` and never
reach the browser page.

Every service and role above was created with Docker and driven through its pskit driver (publish, receive, settle;
put, list, get) during development. Queues and buckets on Azurite, LocalStack, fake-gcs-server and RustFS are created
on first use by the driver (`create_queue` / `create_bucket`), from the host's side, so a firewall between your laptop
and the server doesn't matter and an emulator restart is survived. Extra ports (consoles, Azurite's queue port) move
with the main port: a second RabbitMQ on port 5682 gets its UI on 15682.

title: On-premises: Cluster load balancer
text:
## Load balancer: one URL for the whole cluster (optional)

Add one more saved server **outside** the cluster as its load balancer. pskit runs OpenResty (nginx) there in Docker (container `pskit-lb`, host network) and spreads each deployment's HTTP over the cluster's servers with the algorithm you pick (`--algorithm`: round robin, sticky round robin, weighted round robin, IP hash, least connections (the default) or least time; `--weight edge1=3` per server; see load balancers). It works the same way for all three orchestrators. To share one load balancer between clusters and projects by path instead (`http://lb/<service>/`), attach a named one: `pskit lb attach edge --cluster prod` (load balancers). | Orchestrator | Behind the load balancer | |---|---| | Swarm, k3s | every server (each server's port already reaches every web replica; the load balancer adds one URL and skips a server that is down) | | Nomad | the servers with a web replica, plus the master's main replica when the master serves requests | When the master does **not** serve requests, it is listed on every load balancer as a **backup** only (see below).
### The master and requests | Master serves requests | What happens | |---|---| |

**on** (Swarm / k3s default) | Load balancers spread requests over every server, the master included. Nomad: the master's main replica answers them next to the web replicas. Swarm / k3s: web replicas may also run on the master. Uses the master's spare CPU, but heavy traffic competes with the control plane, schedules, queues and data that live there | | **off** (Nomad default) | The master is idle for requests while a joined server is up: load balancers list it as a `backup` and send it traffic only while every other server is down. Swarm / k3s also keep web replicas off the master (a placement constraint / node affinity) while another server can run them. With no joined server yet, the master still serves everything | Set it when creating the cluster (`--master-serves` / `--no-master-serves`, or the studio switch) and change it any time with `pskit cluster set NAME --master-serves|--no-master-serves` or the switch on the cluster page. The load balancers (the cluster's own and attached named ones) are updated at once. On Swarm and k3s, web replicas move on or off the master at the next `pskit deploy`; so after the first server joins a cluster whose master does not serve, deploy again to move them off the master. Clusters created before this setting keep their old behaviour (off on Nomad, on on Swarm and k3s).

```
                users ──► http://<lb1>/  (nginx on lb1, port 80)
                              │  fewest open connections first
            ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
            ▼                 ▼                 ▼
     edge1 (master)       edge2 (join)      edge3 (join)      :8080 on each
```

title: On-premises: Cluster create, join, scale, and remove
text:
## Commands

| Command | |
|---|---|
| `pskit cluster create NAME -o swarm\|kubernetes\|nomad --master SERVER [--advertise IP] [--[no-]master-serves]` | install on the master and save |
| `pskit cluster join NAME SERVER [--advertise IP]` | add a server (installs, joins, copies images) |
| `pskit cluster set NAME --master-serves\|--no-master-serves` | send requests to the master too, or keep it as a backup only |
| `pskit cluster leave NAME SERVER` | drain and remove a server |
| `pskit cluster status NAME [--json]` | servers, replicas, full or not |
| `pskit cluster check NAME [--no-alert]` | status once and the alert when full (exit 3 when full) |
| `pskit cluster watch NAME [--interval 60]` | check until Ctrl+C |
| `pskit cluster alerts NAME [--function F] [--stage S] [--webhook URL] [--cooldown M] [--cpu/--memory/--disk %] [--test]` | alert settings |
| `pskit cluster scale NAME --replicas N [--stack S]` | web replicas now (until the next deploy) |
| `pskit cluster requests NAME [--follow] [--stack S]` | recent requests, and each server's URL with its share of HTTP |
| `pskit cluster balancer set NAME SERVER [--port 80] [--address IP]` | nginx on a server outside the cluster: one URL for all of it |
| `pskit cluster balancer sync NAME` / `logs NAME [-n 100]` / `remove NAME` | rewrite its config now / its access log / stop it |
| `pskit cluster list` / `pskit cluster remove NAME` | list / forget a cluster |
| `pskit cluster remove NAME --uninstall [--delete-data]` | uninstall the cluster from the master and every server, then forget it |
| `pskit deploy --cluster NAME` / `pskit deploy --server NAME` | deploy the functions to the cluster / to one server |
| `pskit resources onprem create KEY --service S --cluster NAME [--node SERVER]` | a resource on a server of the cluster |

title: On-premises: Swarm, Kubernetes, and Nomad
text:
## How the functions run in a cluster

Each deployment (`pskit-<service>-<stage>`) runs the function host image as two workloads:

* **web** replicas serve your HTTP routes and `invoke()` calls. Adding replicas or servers adds HTTP capacity.
* The **main** replica runs on the master with the data volume. It owns everything stateful: schedules run once,
  not once per replica; built-in queues, topics and buckets live in one place; workflow executions are recorded
  there; queue, storage and topic triggers run there.
* A web replica hands those to main. `submit_queue()`, `put_object()`, workflow starts and `/__pskit/*` admin
  calls are forwarded to it. Its log lines and invocation counts are sent to main every second, tagged with
  `replica`, so `pskit logs`, the studio's **Logs** view and `/__pskit/stats` show the whole cluster.
* Resources with a driver (Redis, SQS, S3, MinIO, ...) are used directly by every replica, as on one server.

Your handler code does not change.

### Nomad does not need a load balancer

Swarm and k3s publish the functions' port on every server and spread HTTP across the web replicas. Nomad does not.
The main replica listens on the master's port. Each web replica listens on its own server's port, one per server.
`pskit deploy` waits until the main replica answers `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/__pskit/health` on the master. That
check does not go through a load balancer, and the deploy succeeds without one.

Send traffic to the master and the main replica handles it. Send traffic to another server and that server's web
replica handles it. For a single URL that spreads requests across the web replicas, let pskit run a
load balancer on one more server, or put your own nginx,
HAProxy or Traefik in front.

While that wait runs, the deploy prints each Nomad allocation and the main replica's logs every 10 seconds, as
they happen. If the port never answers, the output ends with `nomad job status` and those logs.

title: On-premises: Service console
text:
## Console and terminal

Services without a web UI (and those with one) have a **Console**: type a command, see the output.

| Service | Console runs | Try |
|---|---|---|

secret URL; the first start builds a small image (`pskit-terminal:1`, ttyd + OpenSSH + sshpass + docker CLI). Servers
get an SSH session with their saved login; services get their client (or `sh`) through `docker exec`.

title: On-premises: Primary and read replicas
text:
## Databases: one server, or a primary with read replicas - **Single server**: one

container on this machine or a server. To scale it up, give that server more CPU and memory (vertical scaling). Nothing else changes. - **Primary + read replicas** (horizontal scaling): the **primary** takes every write, each **read replica** on another server keeps a copy and answers reads, and an optional **load balancer** gives the functions one address that sends writes to the primary and reads to the replicas. Add replicas later as reads grow. You only pick the servers: which one writes (the primary), which ones read (the replicas) and which one runs the load balancer. Save them first (**Servers**, below). pskit installs Docker where it is missing and sets up replication for each engine: | Engine | Replication | *Synchronous* means | Load balancer (one address) | |---|---|---|---| | PostgreSQL | streaming replication (WAL), each replica starts from `pg_basebackup` | `synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (*)'`: a commit waits until one replica has it on disk | pgpool-II, port 6432 | | MySQL | GTID replication; a replica copies the databases, then follows | semi-synchronous: a commit waits for one replica (async again after 10 s without one) | ProxySQL, port 6033 | | MariaDB | GTID replication, as MySQL | built-in semi-synchronous, as MySQL | ProxySQL, port 6033 | | MongoDB | replica set (`rs_<key>`), members share a generated key file | write concern `w: majority` | none: the driver routes from one replica set URL | **Asynchronous** (default) is the fastest: the primary commits at once and replicas follow a few milliseconds behind, so a crash of the primary can lose the last writes. **Synchronous** loses no committed write, at the cost of a round trip to a replica per commit. PostgreSQL waits while no replica is connected, so keep at least two replicas with *sync*. The load balancer sends writes, transactions and `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` to the primary and plain reads to the replicas, and falls back to the primary only when no replica is up. Without a load balancer, the functions' `URL` is the primary and the replicas are listed in `READ_URLS`. The form draws the result as you pick (functions → load balancer → primary → replicas, solid lines for sync, moving dashes for async). **Details** shows the same picture with each member's state, every replica's lag, what the primary reports (`pg_stat_replication`, `SHOW REPLICAS`, `rs.status()`), and **+ Add read replica** / **Remove**.

```yaml
  name: onprem
  region: local
  options:
    host: 127.0.0.1          # bind address on the *target*. 0.0.0.0 is advertised as 127.0.0.1 unless advertise is set
```

title: On-premises: Load balancer algorithms
text:
## The six algorithms

`pskit lb algorithms` prints the trade-offs. The studio's **Load balancers** page shows the same with a small
animation of each.

| Algorithm | Kind | How it picks a server | Good for | Watch out |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `round_robin` | static | each in turn | servers of the same size, requests of the same cost | ignores load; not sticky |
| `sticky_round_robin` | static | a user's first request picks one; a cookie keeps the session there | in-memory sessions, uploads in parts, WebSockets | busy users make it uneven; sessions move when a server joins or leaves |
| `weighted_round_robin` | static | in turn, `weight` times as often | servers of different sizes | weights are set by hand |
| `ip_hash` | static | the client IP always maps to the same server | sticky without cookies (devices, API clients) | many users behind one NAT land on one server |
| `least_connections` | dynamic | fewest requests in progress (default) | mixed workloads, long requests | a fast and a slow server can look alike |
| `least_time` | dynamic | lowest average response time x requests in progress | latency-sensitive APIs on uneven hardware | can favor one fast server until it slows down |

**Static** algorithms follow a fixed rule; **dynamic** ones measure live load per request. Open-source nginx has
no sticky cookie or least time (both are NGINX Plus), so pskit builds them: sticky hashes a cookie that holds the
first request's id (`hash ... consistent`), and least time runs `balancer_by_lua` with a moving average of each
server's response header time. A server that fails is retried on the next one and rests for 10 s.

`weight` (1..100, per saved server) is used by weighted round robin, least connections and least time.

title: On-premises: Load balancer routes and attach
text:
## Create one and put projects on it A project names it in `pskit.yml`; every `pskit

deploy` updates its route and `pskit remove` drops it: The path prefix is removed before the request reaches your functions (`/shop/orders` arrives as `/orders`) and
sent in `X-Forwarded-Prefix: /shop`. `/shop` redirects to `/shop/`.

A **cluster** can be attached instead; every deployment on it gets `/<service>/` (or `/<service>-<stage>/` when
two stages of a service share the cluster), kept up to date on deploy, remove, join and leave: A project's own `balancer` setting wins over the cluster's route for that deployment. A project whose
placement groups run on several attached clusters gets one route, `/<service>/`, to the servers of
all of them; each server passes another group's routes on to it.

title: On-premises: Monitor services and send alerts
text:
## Monitoring and alerts

The **Servers** list shows a check mark per server: ✓ when its SSH port answers (all probed at once when the list
opens, **Re-check** to probe again), ✗ with the reason otherwise; *Test* replaces it with the result of a full login
check. **Live** on a server shows its CPU, RAM and disk use, refreshed every few seconds, until you switch it off.

A service's **Details** has **Live monitoring**: switch it on to see, every 5 seconds, each container's CPU, memory and
the disk holding its data (for a replicated database: the primary, every replica and the load balancer), the open
connections, the data size and how far each replica is behind. Nothing is measured while it is off.

**Alerts** (optional, in the create form or in Details) send a message when a limit is crossed: CPU, memory or disk
percent of a container, replica lag in seconds, or a container that is down. They go to

- a **function** of the project, run through the deployed host with the alert as `event.data`
  (`{kind: "pskit.database.alert", key, service, reasons, message, sample}`). *Create a new function* adds
  `<key>-alert` to `pskit.yml` with a handler stub; deploy the project to run it;
- a **webhook**: Slack, Teams or Google Chat incoming webhooks show the message; any other URL gets the JSON.

An alert goes out at most once per cooldown (30 minutes by default). The studio checks every minute while it runs;
without it, run the check from cron on any machine with the project:

title: On-premises: Place functions on different servers
text:
# Functions on several servers (on premises)

By default every function of a project runs in one host: on one machine, or on every server of a cluster. **Placement** splits them: each group of functions runs on its own server (or cluster), with only its own code and dependencies, and the groups work together as one project. Per group: one of `server`, `cluster` or `local: true` (the default group may leave it out and use `options.deploy` / `--server` as before), `functions`, and optionally `port` (needed when two groups share a server) and `advertise` (the URL the other groups call, when the server's own address is not reachable). The studio's **Deploy** page has the same editor ("Where functions run"), and each function shows where it runs.
## Each function is its own sub-project

Create functions in their own folder with their own dependencies: The studio does this for new functions ("Own folder with its own requirements.txt"). A function's sub-project is the nearest folder above its handler with a `requirements.txt` (Python) or `package.json` (Node.js). * Every cloud: the sub-projects' requirements are added to the bundle, so the code runs unchanged anywhere. * On premises with placement: **each server installs only the requirements of its functions**, and the folders of functions placed elsewhere are left out of its bundle. Two functions on one server that pin conflicting versions fail the deploy with a clear message: place them on different servers. * Node.js sub-projects get their own `node_modules` in their folder, so each function resolves its own versions.
### Requirements: global plus per function

Each server installs: * the project's `requirements.txt` (global: what every function needs), and * the `requirements.txt` of each of **its** functions' folders (`functions/<name>/requirements.txt`), never those of functions placed elsewhere.
### Functions that share a code file

Each server's copy of a shared code file holds only the handlers of its own functions: pskit removes the others (and the imports only they used) from that group's bundle; your source is not changed. Module-level helpers stay. `pskit_host.json` on the server lists what was removed (`stripped`). Moving them to their own folders is still cleaner, and gives each its own requirements: Functions whose handlers sit side by side in one file (`app/handlers.py` with `hello`, `get_item`, `create_item`, as `pskit init` makes them) are shared code. Validation warns when they are in different groups. Split them: The function, the module-level helpers and imports it uses (relative imports made absolute) move to `functions/<name>/handler.py`. Its `requirements.txt` gets the lines of the project's `requirements.txt` that its imports name, and its handler in `pskit.yml` is updated.

```text
provider:
  name: onprem
  options:
    host: 0.0.0.0
    placement:
      default: api                      # functions not listed here, and every workflow, run in this group
      groups:
        api:   {server: app1}           # a saved server
        gpu:   {server: gpu1, functions: [resize, ocr]}
        batch: {cluster: prod, functions: [report]}             # a scaling cluster ({name: prod, replicas: 3})
        local: {local: true, functions: [dev-tool], port: 8081} # this machine
```

title: On-premises: Portable Python for an on-premises host
text:
# On-premises: Portable Python for an on-premises host

When the server has **no Python**, use `python: bundle` (a portable CPython from python-build-standalone is fetched at apply and copied with the app) or `method: docker` (the image is `FROM python:<minor>-slim`). From Windows, a Linux bundle is copied out of the downloaded archive and is not unpacked into the project (those trees contain test paths longer than `MAX_PATH`). Air-gapped: `python_home` (copy a tree you already have) or `python_url` + `python_sha256` (internal mirror of an `install_only` tarball).

SSH and `scp` write `pskit-run.sh` plus `release.tar.gz` (the staged bundle, `onprem_ctl.py`, `pskit_host.json`, the unit when `install: systemd`, and `python/` when `python: bundle`). With `sudo: true`, apply runs `sudo -n mkdir` on `path` and `chown`s that directory to the SSH user (`deploy` cannot create `/opt/pskit` itself), then copies the files. Apply does not delete `data_dir`. `install: systemd` runs `systemctl restart`. `install: process` runs `onprem_ctl.py start`. Either way the deploy fails if `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/__pskit/health` does not answer, and the failure includes `systemctl status` and `journalctl` when a unit was used.

**Limits:** no cloud authorizer and no IAM mapping. A `terraform.extra` resource from another cloud (`aws_*`, `google_*`, `azurerm_*`, and the other cloud prefixes) is omitted with a warning. A state backend of `s3`, `gcs` or `azurerm` warns; set `provider.state.backend` empty (see `providers.onprem` in examples 11 and 15) to keep state on this machine. Delivery is at-least-once. A missed schedule fires once on the next poll, not as a burst. The host does not kill a handler at `timeout`; `ctx.remaining_time_ms()` still counts down. If `method` is `local` and `provider.runtime` is not the interpreter running `pskit`, validation warns and the host still uses that interpreter. `python: bundle` needs network on first apply unless `python_home` or a cached archive under `~/.cache/pskit/python-standalone` is present. systemd units are written to `/etc/systemd/system` (set `sudo: true` unless the SSH user is root). That `sudo` is non-interactive (`sudo -n`), so the sudoers rule must not ask for a password.

An address or login copied from the source was rewritten in this card. Addresses use 192.0.2.0/24, a documentation range. The login in those examples is deploy.

```text
provider:
  name: onprem
  region: local
  options:
    host: 127.0.0.1          # bind address on the *target*. 0.0.0.0 is advertised as 127.0.0.1 unless advertise is set
    port: 8080               # 1-65535. Give each service its own port
    advertise: https://fn.internal.example   # optional URL written into outputs
    data_dir: .pskit/onprem-data             # default .pskit/onprem-data/<service>-<stage> (local); <path>/data on SSH
    poll_seconds: 0.5
    admin_token: "${env:PSKIT_ADMIN_TOKEN, }"  # header x-pskit-token on /__pskit/* except health
    env_file: .env.onprem      # KEY=VALUE secrets copied next to the host (host.env) and loaded at start;
                               # read by <name>_env driver options and handlers, never written to Terraform state
    execution_retention: 500   # finished workflow executions kept under <data_dir>/executions
    workflow_workers: 8        # workflow runs executing at once; further starts wait for a worker
    log_buffer: 5000           # log entries kept in memory for /__pskit/logs (min 100)
    log_level: INFO            # minimum level captured from `logging`
    capture_output: true       # also record print() / stdout / stderr lines
```

title: On-premises: S3-compatible storage on premises
text:
# On-premises storage (`type: storage`)

Run functions when files appear in a bucket, and read or write objects: the host's built-in buckets, a shared folder, MinIO or another S3-compatible store, or a bucket in a cloud (S3, R2, Azure Blob, GCS, ...). The host lists each watched bucket every `poll_seconds` and compares ETags: a new or changed object emits `created`, a missing one `deleted`. Objects already there at the first start are recorded, not emitted.
## pskit's Amazon S3 compatible server (one click)

*Resources → On-prem services → + Create service → Object storage → Amazon S3 compatible* (`s3` in Python, `s3-node` in Node.js), or the CLI: It runs pskit's own S3 server, whose code is in `aws/s3`, on the stock `python` / `node` image (nothing is built or pushed). Unlike LocalStack it **checks every request's signature** (AWS Signature Version 4 or 2): the service's *user* is the access key ID and its *password* the secret access key. The resource is a `storage` bucket on the `s3` driver (created on first use), so storage triggers work, and the env file gets `PSKIT_<KEY>_URL`, `_ACCESS_KEY` and `_SECRET_KEY` for any other program: It covers the S3 API that applications use: buckets, ListObjects / ListObjectsV2 / ListObjectVersions, put / get / head / delete / copy with ranges, conditions, metadata, tags and checksums (CRC32, CRC32C, CRC64NVME, SHA1, SHA256), multipart uploads, versioning and delete markers, presigned URLs and browser POST uploads, bucket policies (they decide what unsigned requests may do), ACLs, block public access, CORS, lifecycle rules (applied hourly), static website hosting, object lock (retention and legal hold) and default encryption; logging, notification and replication settings are stored. S3 Select, torrents and directory buckets are not supported, and objects are not encrypted at rest. Its **web console** (`http://<server>:<port>/ui/`, *Web UI → S3 console* on the service) signs in with the same user and password: buckets and every bucket setting, folders, drag-and-drop uploads of files and folders, downloads, previews, share links, copy / move / rename, versions (restore an old one), metadata, tags, ACLs and object lock. *Browse → Buckets (S3)* in the studio works on it too. Back it up with *Backup* (a `.tar.gz` of the data volume). Run it without pskit with the Dockerfiles in `aws/s3` (see its README).

```text
resources:
  uploads:
    type: storage                # a directory under data_dir, created at start

functions:
  ingest:
    handler: app.handlers.ingest
    events:
      - storage: {resource: uploads, prefix: in/, suffix: .csv, events: [created, deleted]}
```
